claims.claim: English has two written articles, a/an (indefinite) and the (definite), and the option of using no article at all (zero article); articles modify nouns and signal the kind of reference the noun has.
The indefinite articles a and an signal a non-specific, one-of-many noun and are used with singular count nouns.

The choice between a and an depends on the sound that begins the following word, not its spelling: an hour and an honest answer (silent h, vowel sound), a university and a one-way ticket (y and w consonant sounds), and the rule extends to acronyms such as an MBA program.

The definite article the signals a specific, particular, or unique noun, including nouns identified by shared knowledge, restriction, ordinals, and superlatives, and it combines with singular count, plural count, and noncount nouns.

The zero article is used for generic reference with plural count nouns and noncount nouns and with most proper nouns; named places follow conventions, with the used for rivers, oceans, seas, deserts, regions, and collections such as the Great Lakes and the Netherlands.
In connected text, a noun introduced for the first time typically takes a or an, and later reference to the same noun takes the.

Articles interact with countability: a/an occurs only with singular count nouns; the occurs with singular count, plural count, and noncount nouns; zero article occurs with plural count and noncount nouns for indefinite or generic reference.
Names of languages, sports, and academic subjects take no article in their general sense (French, basketball, chemistry).

Common learner errors include omitting the with identifiable nouns, adding the to generic nouns, choosing a or an by spelling instead of sound, and using a or an with plural or noncount nouns; all have predictable corrections.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Grammar traditions differ on how to classify articles: a separate part of speech, a kind of adjective, or a member of the determiner class.
positions: eCampusOntario Language Foundations defines an article as a type of adjective used before a noun
other frameworks treat articles as determiners alongside this, that, some, and any
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the article system on its own terms and notes that some traditions group articles differently, consistent with the sibling parts-of-speech lesson.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Generic reference can be expressed with more than one article pattern (plural with zero article, singular with the, or singular with a/an as a representative example).
positions: zero article with plural and noncount nouns is the most general pattern
the plus singular noun is common in technical and scientific writing
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches plural and noncount zero-article generics as the primary pattern and does not present the plus singular as the only option.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Countability conventions vary across languages and varieties of English (for example, advice, information, and research are noncount in American English but count in some other languages).
positions: countability is a property of the noun as used in a variety
a learner's first language may classify nouns differently
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson notes the variation and points learners to dictionary checking, framing article difficulty as a natural system difference rather than a learner deficiency.
